title: Election Day
subtitle: Federal elections, ridings, who can vote, Elections Canada and the secret ballot

questions.question: Under legislation passed by Parliament, when must federal elections be held?
options: On the first Tuesday of November every four years
On the third Monday in October every four years following the most recent general election
questions.explanation: Federal elections must be held on the third Monday in October every four years following the most recent general election. The Prime Minister may ask the Governor General to call an earlier election.

questions.question: What is an electoral district?
options: A geographical area represented by a member of Parliament, also called a riding or constituency
questions.explanation: An electoral district, also known as a riding or constituency, is a geographical area represented by a member of Parliament. The guide lists 308 districts; after the 2022 redistribution there are 343.

questions.question: How many electoral districts (ridings) does the guide say Canada is divided into?
questions.explanation: The guide says Canada is divided into 308 electoral districts. Note that the number has since grown: 338 ridings from 2015 and 343 from the 2025 election onward.

questions.question: Who may run as a candidate in a federal election?
options: Canadian citizens who are 18 years old or older
Only members of a registered political party
questions.explanation: Canadian citizens who are 18 years old or older may run in a federal election. The people who run for office are called candidates, and there can be many in an electoral district.

questions.question: How does a candidate become the MP for an electoral district?
options: By receiving the most votes in that district
By receiving more than 50% of all votes nationwide
By being chosen by the party leader
By appointment of the Governor General
questions.explanation: The people in each electoral district vote for the candidate and party of their choice. The candidate who receives the most votes becomes the MP for that electoral district.

questions.question: Who is entitled to vote in a Canadian federal election?
options: Anyone living in Canada for more than a year
A Canadian citizen, at least 18 years old on voting day, and on the voters' list
questions.explanation: You are eligible to vote in a federal election or referendum if you are a Canadian citizen, at least 18 years old on voting day, and on the voters' list.

questions.question: Which neutral agency of Parliament produces the voters' lists from the National Register of Electors?
questions.explanation: The voters' lists are produced from the National Register of Electors by a neutral agency of Parliament called Elections Canada, a permanent database of citizens 18 and over qualified to vote.

questions.question: What is the voter information card?
options: A card mailed by Elections Canada telling you when and where to vote
A membership card for a political party
questions.explanation: Once an election is called, Elections Canada mails a voter information card to each elector in the National Register. It lists when and where you vote and a number to call for an interpreter or special services.

questions.question: What should you do if you do not receive a voter information card?
options: You cannot vote in that election
Call your local elections office or Elections Canada to ensure you are on the voters' list
Vote at any polling station without identification
questions.explanation: If you do not receive a card, call your local elections office or Elections Canada. You can be added to the voters' list at any time, including on election day.

questions.question: When you go to vote on election day, what do you do?
options: Show your passport and sign a register
Go to your polling station, bring your voter information card and proof of identity and address, mark an X beside your candidate behind the screen, and deposit the ballot in the box
Tell the poll official your choice out loud
questions.explanation: Go to the polling station on your voter information card with proof of identity and address. Behind the screen, mark an "X" in the circle next to the candidate of your choice, fold the ballot, present it to the poll officials, who tear off the number, and deposit it in the ballot box.

questions.question: How do you mark a federal election ballot?
options: Mark an "X" in the circle next to the name of the candidate of your choice
questions.explanation: Mark an "X" in the circle next to the name of the candidate of your choice.

questions.question: If you cannot or do not wish to vote on election day, what are your options?
options: Vote at the advance polls or by special ballot
Ask a family member to vote for you
questions.explanation: If you cannot or do not wish to vote on election day, you can vote at the advance polls or by special ballot. The dates and location are on your voter information card.

questions.question: In Canada, are you obliged to tell other people how you voted?
options: Yes, if a family member asks
No. Voting is secret; no one, including family, employer or union, has the right to insist you tell them
Only if you are a public servant
questions.explanation: Canadian law secures the right to a secret ballot. You may choose to discuss how you voted, but no one, including family members, your employer or union representative, has the right to insist that you tell them.

questions.question: What happens immediately after the polling stations close?
options: Ballots are sealed for a month
Election officers count the ballots and results are announced on radio, television and in newspapers
The Governor General counts the votes
questions.explanation: Immediately after the polling stations close, election officers count the ballots and the results are announced on radio and television and in the newspapers, and on the Elections Canada website.

questions.question: True or false: Permanent residents may vote in Canadian federal elections.
questions.explanation: False. Only Canadian citizens who are at least 18 on voting day and on the voters' list may vote in federal elections. Voting is one of the privileges of citizenship.

questions.question: True or false: You can still be added to the voters' list on election day itself.
questions.explanation: True. Even if you are not in the National Register of Electors or did not receive a card, you can be added to the voters' list at any time, including on election day.

questions.question: True or false: The rules for voting in provincial, territorial and municipal elections are exactly the same as for federal elections.
questions.explanation: False. Provincial, territorial and municipal elections are held by secret ballot, but the rules are not the same as for federal elections. It is important to find out the local rules.
questions.ref: Discover Canada, Other Levels of Government (p. 33)

questions.question: True or false: The Prime Minister may ask the Governor General to call an election earlier than the fixed date.
questions.explanation: True. Although elections are fixed for the third Monday in October every four years, the Prime Minister may ask the Governor General to call an earlier election.

questions.question: What does the poll official do with your ballot after you have marked it?
options: Tears off the ballot number and gives the ballot back to you to deposit in the ballot box
questions.explanation: The poll official will tear off the ballot number and give your ballot back to you to deposit in the ballot box. This keeps your vote secret while preventing fraud.

questions.question: Members of the House of Commons are also known as what?
questions.explanation: Canadians vote for the people they want to represent them in the House of Commons. Members of the House of Commons are also known as members of Parliament or MPs.
